page: Amazon Web Services m5n.8xlarge is a general-purpose instance type optimized for network and EBS throughput. It is powered by an Intel Xeon 8259CL processor with an x86_64 architecture, running at a clock speed of 3.1 GHz. The instance features 32 dedicated vCPUs derived from 16 physical cores with hyperthreading enabled. It is equipped with 128.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, providing a resource density of 4.0 GB of RAM per core. This instance does not include local storage or GPU hardware, relying entirely on network-attached storage.

Benchmark results indicate a clear distinction between single-core and multi-core capabilities. Single-core performance is relatively weak, falling into the bottom 25% for stress-ng, gzip compression, and Geekbench single-core tests. However, multi-core execution scales to average levels, as demonstrated by the Passmark CPU score of 26,438.58 and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression. Memory bandwidth remains consistently in the middle 50% tier, reaching 105.41 GB/sec for large-block read operations and 46.68 GB/sec for write operations.

Operating on the Nitro hypervisor, the instance provides a baseline network bandwidth of 25 Gbps. It supports AVX-512 vector instructions, which assist in cryptographic and mathematical operations, yielding average performance in Passmark encryption and physics tests. For workloads, the instance is suited for multi-threaded applications such as static web serving, database operations, and small-to-medium language model inference, though it exhibits poor performance on larger 70B parameter models. The primary tradeoff lies in its moderate single-core processing speed compared to its robust multi-core scaling and high network throughput.
description: Amazon Web Services m5n.8xlarge is a general-purpose, network-optimized instance featuring 32 dedicated vCPUs and 128.0 GB of DDR4 memory. Powered by an Intel Xeon 8259CL processor running at 3.1 GHz on the Nitro hypervisor, it delivers a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. The instance lacks local storage and GPUs, relying on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 25 Gbps. Benchmark data shows weak single-core performance, but average multi-core and memory bandwidth capabilities, with a Passmark CPU score of 26,438.58 and a Redis SET throughput of 25.86 million operations per second. It is suited for multi-threaded workloads, database operations, static web serving, and small-to-medium LLM inference, though it exhibits poor performance on larger models.
